stemMd: A row has three switches, initially all off. An operation reverses exactly two switches. Can a sequence of operations leave exactly one switch on?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Yes, by reversing two overlapping pairs.

options.label: B
options.textMd: No, because no switch can ever turn on.

options.label: C
options.textMd: No, because the number of on switches always remains even.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Yes, by reversing the same pair twice.

options.label: E
options.textMd: Yes, by reversing each pair once.

explanationMd: Flipping two bits changes the number of on switches by 2, 0 or minus 2. Its parity stays even from the initial zero, so one on switch is impossible.

distractorRationale.d: That returns the pair to its starting state.
distractorRationale.a: That leaves two switches on, not one.
distractorRationale.e: Each switch is reversed twice and ends off.
distractorRationale.b: One operation turns two switches on.
